summary: This informational document outlines how existing IPv6 protocols can give each host its own unique IPv6 prefix rather than one address from a shared prefix. Benefits include better host isolation and easier management of individual subscribers.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of every house sharing one street, each gets its own whole street. That keeps neighbors apart and makes it easier to keep track of who is who.

questions: how to give each host its own ipv6 prefix
how to assign unique ipv6 prefixes per host
subtitle: Give each device its own IPv6 street, not just an address on a shared one.

tldr.problem: When many devices connect to a shared network (like hotel or airport Wi-Fi), operators need to isolate them from each other to prevent attacks and manage usage fairly. Standard IPv6 addressing gives each device an address from a shared prefix, but this does not prevent direct device-to-device attacks on shared links.
tldr.mechanism: Instead of giving all devices addresses from one shared /64 prefix, the first-hop router assigns each device its own unique /64 prefix and configures router advertisements so that devices cannot reach each other directly—they must go through the router. This leverages existing IPv6 protocols (SLAAC, Router Advertisements) without requiring new standards.
tldr.outcome: Shared networks gain automatic protection against link-level attacks like Neighbor Discovery spoofing, and operators can apply per-device policies (bandwidth limits, access controls) using the prefix as an anchor point.

today: RFC 8273 is an Informational RFC published in December 2017. It documents best current practices for operator-managed shared-access networks and has not been obsoleted. The guidance comes from large-scale production deployments and remains applicable to modern wireless and wired shared network scenarios.

sections.title: The Challenge of Shared Networks
sections.content:
Many networks allow multiple devices to connect at the same physical level—hotel Wi-Fi, airport networks, shared data center subnets. A shared-access network connects many independent, temporary visitors. The network operator often has a legal or practical requirement to isolate devices from each other so that one guest's device cannot attack another's or consume unfair bandwidth.

In IPv4 this is easier because the network assigns individual addresses. In IPv6, the standard approach gives multiple devices addresses from a single shared prefix (like 2001:db8::/64). When devices are on the same link and share a prefix, IPv6's Neighbor Discovery protocol allows them to communicate directly, which opens up various attack vectors including spoofed Neighbor Advertisements and rogue Router Advertisements.

This RFC describes a method to isolate devices using only existing IPv6 protocols, without needing new standards.
sections.plainLanguage: When people share a Wi-Fi network, their devices can sometimes trick each other or interfere. This RFC says how to keep them apart using only the tools IPv6 already has.

sections.title: How to Isolate Devices
sections.content:
The first-hop router—the L3 edge device directly connected to visiting devices—assigns each device its own unique /64 prefix instead of giving all devices addresses from one /64. When a device asks for an IPv6 prefix (via a Router Solicitation message), the router answers with a unique prefix. The key to isolation is the L-bit in the IPv6 Router Advertisement: when the L-bit is unset (off), the destination prefix is not considered 'on-link,' which means the device will not try to reach other devices on the same physical link directly. Instead, by RFC 4861 rules, the device must route all external traffic through the first-hop router.

The router achieves this by unicasting Router Advertisements to each device (using the device's link-layer address) instead of multicast, ensuring only the device receiving the prefix sees that particular advertisement. Combined with stateless DHCPv6 for optional configuration (like DNS server addresses), the setup allows devices to auto-configure their addresses using SLAAC (Stateless Address Autoconfiguration) while being forced to route through the operator's gateway.
sections.plainLanguage: The router gives each device its own prefix and tells it 'your neighbors are not on this link'—so every message has to come back through me. That way neighbors can't talk directly.

sections.title: Router Advertisement Flags
sections.content:
The RFC specifies recommended values for the flags in IPv6 Router Advertisements on shared networks. The M-flag (managed) is set to 0, indicating addresses are not managed by DHCPv6. The A-flag (autonomous) is set to 1, allowing devices to auto-configure themselves using SLAAC. The O-flag (other) is set to 1, allowing stateless DHCPv6 for 'other' information like DNS server addresses. Most importantly, the L-flag (on-link) is set to 0, which prevents devices from assuming destinations matching the prefix are on-link.

Each device receives its own unique /64 prefix in these advertisements. The router must send solicited RAs (replies to Router Solicitations) to the subscriber's unicast link-layer address, and optionally unsolicited periodic RAs as well, to keep prefix lifetimes fresh. This configuration ensures the broadest compatibility across different device operating systems while providing isolation.
sections.plainLanguage: The router says: 'Here is your prefix. Use it to pick your own address. Ask for DNS if you need it. But anything outside needs to go through me.'

sections.title: Address Assignment and Verification
sections.content:
After receiving a Router Advertisement with a unique prefix and the A-flag set, a device configures itself with a 128-bit address within that prefix using SLAAC. The device generates the address (usually by combining the prefix with its interface identifier) and then runs the Duplicate Address Detection (DAD) algorithm to ensure no other device is using that address. Because each device has its own prefix, a collision within that device's prefix space is extremely unlikely; however, DAD runs for each address the device chooses.

The device then uses that address to communicate with the router and the wider network. Because the L-bit is unset, any communication with hosts outside the device's own prefix goes through the router, providing isolation from other devices on the shared link.
sections.plainLanguage: Each device picks an address within its own prefix and checks that no one else is using it. Then it is ready to talk to the outside world, but only through the router.

sections.title: Neighbor Discovery and Operational Considerations
sections.content:
When using stateless IPv6 address assignment with SLAAC, the router must carefully manage prefix lifetimes. Preferred and valid lifetimes indicate when a prefix (and its addresses) should be used; the router extends these by sending unsolicited Router Advertisements. The RFC recommends a maximum Router Advertisement interval (MaxRtrAdvInterval) of 300 seconds under normal conditions, or up to 686 seconds when serving many battery-powered devices to save their energy.

Since the router does not receive explicit notifications when devices stop using a prefix, operators may see many stale entries in the router's neighbor table. The RFC recommends quickly removing stale neighbor state to conserve memory. It also notes that some devices will attempt to use IPv6 privacy extensions (RFC 4941), which generate temporary addresses; the router must handle multiple globally routable addresses from the same device.
sections.plainLanguage: The router has to keep refreshing the prefix information so devices do not forget it. And the router should clean up old device entries so its memory does not fill up.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Implications
sections.content:
Unique prefixes per host provide strong isolation against link-level attacks such as Neighbor Discovery cache exhaustion, rogue Router Advertisements, and Duplicate Address Detection spoofing. However, when combined with IPv6 privacy extensions (which generate temporary 'private' addresses), privacy is reduced: a prefix may be associated with a subscriber even when that subscriber is using privacy addresses, allowing a remote observer to track the subscriber by following its prefix. If a subscriber wishes to maintain privacy, they should randomize their link-layer (MAC) address when connecting.

This is an Informational RFC presenting best current practices for shared networks. It originated from a large-scale production deployment and has not been obsoleted. The RFC recommends using SLAAC rather than stateful DHCPv6 IA_NA for maximum compatibility with different device implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: Isolation protects you from your neighbors, but your prefix identifies you. If you want real privacy, change your device's link-layer address too.
